person.note:
See [BAQ9MH4T]: 193 for the main events of his life.
Three manuscript editions of his writings and translations were deposited respectively in rNgog Blo ldan shes rab's tomb, in the monastery of gSang phu (probably in the main assembly hall), and in Drin las kyi sde (ID:4357) ([7FZ3B926]: 107).

person.note:
The majority of the information available on Phya pa has been provided in [EZ5JXHJY] and [8S7FDMCJ]. Summaries of the same are also found in [LQZU66YX]: 37-40, [F4UK2S8P]: 2-3, and [BW9UR427]: 35-36 (in French).
On his birth in 1109, the year of rNgog Blo ldan shes rab (ID:3786)'s passing, see [TM8DW8WA]: 32-33, [VKBZTBWN]: 4b4-5, and [8GL7ZT7Y]: 15b2-3. On the date of his passing in a "sa mo glang" year, see [R894SIKE]: 400, [VKBZTBWN]: 4b4-5 and 6a5. [95UZA9Y5]: 40/3/5 (reported in [7FZ3B926]: 111 and [MPRU5QUC]: 206) specifies the day "sa mo glang gi lo'i nag pa zla ba nag po'i phyogs kyi tshes brgyad," i.e., on the 23rd of the third month.
A list of his students is provided in [EZ5JXHJY]: 356, based on [MQB8JGAX]: 297/4, [KL9XTQWI]: I, 454, [4YEPFBIB]: 340-341, [8GL7ZT7Y], fol. 15b3, [VKBZTBWN], fol. 4b7-5a4. [FDEWZ2NZ]: 290 also mentions the list of the four "jo sras" from bSod nams dpal's Bla ma rngog pa yab sras rim par byon pa’i rnam thar rin po che’i rgyan gyi phreng ba.
'Gos lo tsa ba lists numerous works composed before Phya pa took the see of gSang phu; these include commentaries and summaries on the Five works of Maitreya, the Pramāṇaviniścaya, the Satyadvayavibhaṅga, Madhyamakālaṃkāra, Madhyamakāloka, and Bodhicaryāvatāra. He mentions having seen these, the Yid kyi mun sel (ID:4503) and summaries on Madhyamaka, as well as (ID:4505) and (ID:5971). See exX0032026-04-2304-02-58 . 'Gos lo tsa ba does not mention any composition dealing with monastic discipline.
Śākya mchog ldan ([TM8DW8WA], 12-13 and 32) mentions a (doubtful) commentary on the Pramāṇavārttika (ID:3772) in addition to the commentary on the Pramāṇaviniścaya, and three summaries (small, intermediate, large), the intermediate one being the Yid kyi mun sel (ID:4503). (Discussed in [EZ5JXHJY]: 357, translated in [8S7FDMCJ]: 59).
Four groups of students are mentioned in Tibetan sources (which do not imply that the members of the respective groups were studying with Phya pa at the same time), with occasional variations:
1) The "Eight Great Lions" (seng chen brgyad). Eight scholars whose names contains the expression "seng ge," likely connoting their expertise in epistemology. The standard list includes gTsang nag pa (ID:3839), Dan 'bag (ID:3840), 'Bru sha (ID:3841), rMa bya (ID:3842), rTsags/rTsegs (ID:4289), Myang/Nyang bran (ID:3844), and gNyal pa/dMyal ma (ID:6679). The eighth one is instead sometimes said to be gTsang pa 'Jam dpal (ID:6336), 'U yug pa (ID:3846), or mTshur ston (DI:4315).
2) The "four sons of noble families" (jo sras mi bzhi) or the "three sons of noble families" (jo sras gsum). They are young noble men of the rNgog (ID:3847), 'Khon (ID:3848), Khu (ID:3849), and gNyos/sMyos (ID:3850). The four are listed in [VKBZTBWN]: 4a7 and [8GL7ZT7Y]: 15b3, whereas on 16a1 the author speaks of "jo sras gsum." The four are also listed by bSod nams dpal, see [FDEWZ2NZ]: 290.
3) The "three wise ones" (shes rab can mi gsum) or "four wise ones" (shes rab can mi bzhi). The threefold-list in [VKBZTBWN]: 5a1 has rKong po (ID:3852), lHo pa sgom gzan (ID:3853), Par bu ba/sPar phu ba (ID:3854). 'Gar dbang grub (ID:3851) is added in the fourfold list, e.g. in [R894SIKE]: 406.
4) The "three accomplished ones" (grub thob mi gsum). These are students who later became famous masters: Dus gsum mkhyen pa (ID:3855), Phag mo gru pa (ID:3856), gSal sto (ID:3857). The third is sometimes replaced by Zhang tshal (ID:6409), or is suggested to be the latter's direct student.

person.persName: bla ma dam pa bsod nams rgyal mtshan
bcom ldan rigs pa'i ral gri
person.note: On his career, see [KHA9ZVGP]: 3-8. The dates 1227-1305 are known from the biography (see work (ID:7016)) composed by his student bSam gtan bzang po (ID:4005) ([KHA9ZVGP]: 3). His name in religion was Dar ma rgyal mtshan or Chos kyi rgyal mtshan ([FZ6N88AU]: 406) - the name Chos kyi rgyal mtshan is given as his "real name" (mtshan dngos) in a homage by Rong ston ([KM47ZZDJ]: 657 and n. 62). The majority of the colophons of his works name him "bCom ldan ral gri," a few "Rigs/Rig pa’i ral gri" or just "Ral gri." Schwabland's discussion of the variants “Rigs pa” and “Rig pa” does not come to a definite conclusion as to which is the correct spelling ([CTQMVBPR]: 2-3). He was born as the son of a local wealthy headman, the fourth of five sons and his birth is reported to have been foretold by Śākyaśrībhadra (ID:6418) when he was invited by Ral gri's paternal uncle ([KHA9ZVGP]: 3).

bibl.author: gnas drug pa blo gros mtshungs med
bibl.note:
As the author completed the work in Sa skya (ID:5733), refers to Phyogs glang gsar ma (ID:6828), and mostly follows the Rigs gter (ID:5564), he is to be identified as Blo gros mtshungs med gNas drug pa (ID:4094) rather than Blo gros mtshungs med gSang phu ba (ID:3896).
This work might be the "tshad ma bsdus pa" referred to in the biography of Mi nyag 'Jam dbyangs grags pa ([FEHIEFEB]: 141). [8H6M69W4], No. 16323 mistakenly indicates "mnga' ris kyi dge ba'i bshes gnyen 'od zer seng ge" as the author, whereas he is the person who offered the paper to write down the text.
The author makes an opposition between the "rigs gter ba" (followers of the Rigs gter (ID:5564)) and the "bsdus par smra ba," "bsdus pa ba," or "bod bsdus smra ba" (followers of the [Tibetan] summaries). He frequently refers anonymously to the views of Tibetan scholars. In particular, he regularly compares the views of Chu mig pa (ID:4018) and bCom ldan ral gri (ID:4006), without naming the proponents of the views in question (e.g., ex087042026-02-2316-10-18 ). The author however explicitly names Phya pa (ID:3831), Chu mig pa (ID:4018) and his followers, Sa skya Paṇḍita (ID:3892), and rNgog Lo tsa ba (ID:3786)'s followers.
